chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
title: No guitar solos with Nat; the album After Midnight
summary: Not being allowed to solo frustrated Collins and drove him to practice harder; he got several solos on the 1959 album After Midnight.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: You were much stronger with Cole though than anybody else in that group.
Well, Charlie was not -- neither one of them were solos, no. As a matter of fact Charlie was a very good musician, Lee was a very good musician, also. But no soloist. You know.
Actually it was probably more frustrat-
ing to you than for them.

Oh, it used to kill me sometimes. You know, because especially because I had quite a reputation too, you know, and people would expect me to play, and no guitar solo. And that was kind of frustrating. So it only -- I'll tell you what it did, though. It made me just study that much and practice that much harder, you know, because I --

Yeah, I had to do it -- yeah, so I would go home and just really get into it every night, and really practice and study, because I knew that when I left there I had to cut it. And I had so much to say, I had to get it out. And so I would go to my room and get it out, you know. But it was just, as I said, one of those things. Speaking of recording, one recording I did with Nat also was an album called 'After Midnight.' And I had quite a few solos in this album, which I liked. This album featured Edison Hugh Tizol Harry 'Sweets' Addison, Warren Tzole, and Stuff Smith. It's a tremendous album.
Capitol, yeah. So I got quite a few things to play on here. I don't know how that happened but I slipped through.
